# Zero Trust Requires Whole-Agency Scope — Network, CSPs, and VMware as One System

## Why a whole-agency Zero Trust score requires one naming and identity plane across Network, every CSP, and VMware — and why even Microsoft's own assessment tools, run together, don't add up to whole-agency coverage

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}

:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Companion paper.** This paper is a focused extension of *[Zero Trust
Governance Principles](zero-trust-governance-principles.qmd)*, which sets out
five governance principles for closing the gap between CISA's Zero Trust
Maturity Model (ZTMM) v2.0 cross-cutting capabilities — Visibility and
Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and Governance — and where most
federal programs actually stall. That paper's Principle One establishes
identity as the addressing root the other pillars resolve against. This paper
takes that principle to its whole-agency conclusion: Network, every cloud
service provider (CSP), and any on-premises virtualization estate all have to
resolve against the *same* naming and identity plane before a Zero Trust score
covering them means the same thing across all three — and even Microsoft's own
assessment tooling, run in full, does not get an agency there on its own. Read
the companion paper first for the full governance argument this one builds on;
read this one on its own if the question in front of you is specifically
whether a "whole-agency" Zero Trust score is real.
:::

### Executive summary

Federal agencies routinely assess Network, cloud service providers, and
on-premises virtualization (VMware and similar hypervisor estates) as three
separate exercises, then staple the resulting reports together and call the
result a "whole-agency" Zero Trust maturity score. It isn't one — it's three
partial assessments wearing one cover page. The reason is architectural, not
organizational: NIST SP 800-207 defines the Zero Trust policy decision as
infrastructure-agnostic, which only holds if Network, every CSP, and any
virtualization estate resolve to the *same* asset, naming, and identity
records. When they don't, the same physical workload can appear as three
different objects to three different assessors, and no score computed across
them is measuring one architecture. This paper works through why that's true,
why the hypervisor case is a distinct threat class rather than a naming
inconvenience, why the unification layer itself becomes the highest-value
target in the estate once it exists, and — as a concrete worked example —
why even Microsoft's own SCuBA/ScubaGear and Zero Trust Assessment tools,
run together and scoped only to Microsoft's ecosystem, still fall short of
a whole-agency answer.

### 1. Why this needs to be assessed as one system, not three

Federal Zero Trust programs routinely inventory and assess Network, cloud
service providers (CSPs), and on-premises virtualization (VMware and similar
hypervisor estates) as three separate exercises — a network team's TIC 3.0
boundary review, a cloud security team's per-CSP posture scan, and a
virtualization team's hypervisor hardening checklist — each producing its own
report, on its own schedule, to its own owner. A "whole-agency" Zero Trust
maturity score assembled by stapling these three reports together is not a
whole-agency assessment. It is three partial assessments wearing one cover
page — the same "assess before you've unified" mistake the companion paper's
governance principles argue against in general, applied here across
infrastructure domains instead of within one of them: a scan can only confirm
that an architecture is unified, and cannot substitute for unifying it.

Two documented incidents anchor the argument that follows, both discussed at
greater length in the companion paper. In 2023, a China-based actor tracked
as Storm-0558 stole a Microsoft signing key and forged authentication tokens,
reading email at roughly 25 organizations — including the U.S. Department of
State and Department of Commerce — for weeks before detection; the federal
Cyber Safety Review Board called the breach "preventable." Separately, the
February 2023 "ESXiArgs" ransomware campaign (CVE-2021-21974) and a July 2024
VMware ESXi Active Directory-integration authentication bypass
(CVE-2024-37085) both compromised a layer that sits *beneath* every guest
workload's own telemetry: an attacker who compromises ESXi or vCenter can
encrypt or exfiltrate every VM on the host without a single guest-OS-level
EDR, identity, or network control ever generating an alert, because none of
them observe the hypervisor layer. CVE-2024-37085 in particular turned on
ESXi trusting an Active Directory group's *name*, not a continuously
re-verified, non-recreatable identity — an attacker with sufficient AD
permissions could delete and recreate the "ESX Admins" group and inherit
full hypervisor administrative rights.

### 2. Whole-agency scope: Network, CSPs, and VMware are one system, not three

The root issue is architectural, not organizational: Network, every CSP an
agency operates in, and any on-premises virtualization estate all have to
resolve against **the same naming and identity plane** before any of them can
produce evidence that means the same thing as the others'. NIST SP 800-207
states the Zero Trust core logic — a policy engine evaluating subject
identity, device state, and resource sensitivity together, the same logic the
companion paper's Principle One (§4) develops in depth — as
infrastructure-agnostic by design: the policy decision does not change
because a workload happens to run on-network, in a CSP, or on a
virtualization hypervisor. If an agency's Network, CSP, and VMware estates
each maintain independent asset inventories, independent naming, and
independent identity assertions, that infrastructure-agnostic policy logic
has nothing consistent to evaluate — the same physical workload can appear
as three different objects to three different assessors.

**The hypervisor case is not just a naming problem — it is a distinct threat
class.** As the incidents recapped in §1 show, ESXiArgs (CVE-2021-21974) and
the ESXi AD-integration bypass (CVE-2024-37085) both compromise a layer that
sits *beneath* every guest workload's own telemetry: an attacker who
compromises ESXi or vCenter can encrypt or exfiltrate every VM on the host
without a single guest-OS-level EDR, identity, or network control ever
generating an alert, because none of them observe the hypervisor layer. This
has a direct implication for the "resolve to the same identity plane"
principle above: vCenter's Single Sign-On domain is frequently its **own**
identity source, federated (if at all) into the agency's broader identity
plane as a deliberate integration project with its own risk — CVE-2024-37085
is precisely a case where that federation (trusting an AD group by name) was
the exploited weakness, not a hardening the federation added. Unifying
VMware into the agency identity plane is the right target state; treating it
as already accomplished, or as a low-risk configuration change, is not.

Three architectural facts a whole-agency program has to reconcile before
assessing:

1. **One authoritative asset inventory, not three.** NIST 800-53's CM-8
   (System Component Inventory) and CISA's Binding Operational Directive 23-01
   (asset and vulnerability visibility) both require a single, authoritative
   accounting of what the agency operates — not "the network team's asset
   list, the cloud team's tag taxonomy, and the virtualization team's
   inventory, reconciled manually at audit time." Every CSP an agency
   operates in, and any VMware or equivalent virtualization estate, has to
   resolve to the same asset identity the network layer already tracks.
2. **One naming and address-resolution authority, not per-platform DNS/DHCP/IPAM.**
   NIST SC-20/21/22 (secure, resilient name and address resolution) apply the
   same requirement regardless of whether a workload sits on-network, behind
   a CSP's native DNS, or on a virtualized overlay network. Per-platform
   naming reconciled after the fact — rather than authoritative from a single
   source before the fact — is exactly the "solve it at audit time" pattern
   that produces reactive remediation instead of the continuous evidence the
   companion paper's Principle Three (§6) argues governance has to deliver.
3. **VPN-perimeter thinking does not extend to any of the three.** A
   site-to-site VPN, a CSP's default virtual-network boundary, and a flat
   virtualized network segment are, architecturally, the same mistake: each
   extends implicit trust to everyone already inside a network boundary,
   which is precisely what CISA's ZTMM Networks pillar and NIST SP 800-207
   both define Zero Trust against. Micro-segmentation and policy enforcement
   have to apply identically whether the workload is on-premises, in any CSP,
   or in a virtualized cluster — an agency that Zero-Trust-segments its cloud
   workloads but leaves its on-premises virtualization estate on a flat,
   VPN-reachable network has not solved the root issue; it has moved it.

**A fourth fact the first three create and do not resolve on their own: the
unification layer itself becomes the highest-value target in the estate.** A
single authoritative Network + CSP + VMware naming/identity plane is, by
construction, a complete asset map of the agency's entire attack surface and
— if it also carries reconciliation privileges across all three domains — a
privileged-access broker in its own right. An agency that builds this
unification and does not separately harden it has built the single most
attractive target in its own architecture and left it undefended. At
minimum, governance for the unification layer itself requires: its
administrative access treated under the privileged-identity controls the
companion paper's Principle Two (§5) sets out (time-boxed, independently
verified, not standing); its own high-priority telemetry stream, monitored
distinctly from the domains it unifies; and a blast-radius design that
assumes the unification layer will eventually be targeted directly, not only
reached through one of the three domains it reconciles.

(As the companion paper's Principle Three notes about Binding Operational
Directive 25-01 (§6): BOD 25-01 is M365-specific and doesn't itself extend to
CSPs, network, or VMware — this section's argument rests on the
infrastructure-agnostic NIST 800-207/CM-8/SC-20-22 controls, not on the
directive's legal scope.)

**The practical consequence:** an agency cannot honestly claim whole-agency
Zero Trust maturity by running a cloud-configuration assessor against its
CSPs, a separate posture scan against its network boundary, and a separate
hardening checklist against its VMware estate, then presenting three passing
reports as one score. Each report is real and each is useful — but "whole
agency" requires the identity and naming unification in points 1–3 above to
exist **first**, so that the three assessments measure the same underlying
architecture rather than three architecturally disconnected estates that
happen to share a compliance deadline.

### 3. A worked example: why even Microsoft's own tools don't add up to "whole agency"

Two free, read-only Microsoft-ecosystem assessment tools illustrate the §2
principle concretely, because federal agencies routinely treat them as
interchangeable, or as together constituting full Zero Trust coverage — both
are mistakes, in opposite directions:

| | CISA SCuBA / ScubaGear | Microsoft's Zero Trust Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Question it answers | Compliance — is our M365 configuration aligned with the federal baseline? | Maturity — how close is our environment to Zero Trust? |
| Federal mandate? | Yes — BOD 25-01 requires deploying it against every in-scope M365 tenant, integrating with CISA's continuous-monitoring feed, and remediating deviations | No — it is Microsoft's own guidance, not a federal directive |
| Scope | M365 workloads: Exchange Online, Defender for Office 365, SharePoint/OneDrive, Teams, Power Platform | Broader Microsoft cloud: Entra identity, Intune (devices), Azure, Microsoft Purview (data) |
| Where they overlap | Almost entirely Entra identity — legacy authentication, MFA, Conditional Access, privileged-role hygiene, risky users | Same identity surface, evaluated at greater depth than SCuBA's prescriptive baseline |

Outside identity the two barely touch the same ground: SCuBA owns Exchange,
Defender for Office 365, Teams, and Power Platform, none of which the Zero
Trust Assessment evaluates at all; the Zero Trust Assessment owns Intune
devices, Azure infrastructure, and Purview data, none of which SCuBA
evaluates. Running only one of the two leaves the other's workloads
unassessed — dropping SCuBA because "the Zero Trust Assessment covers
identity" leaves Exchange, Teams, and Power Platform unassessed against the
federal baseline; dropping the Zero Trust Assessment because "SCuBA already
runs" leaves devices, Azure, and data entirely unmeasured.

But running **both**, fully, still does not produce a whole-agency Zero Trust
assessment — because both tools, however complementary, are scoped to one
vendor's ecosystem. §2 already established why: Network, every CSP, and any
on-premises virtualization estate have to reconcile to one authoritative
naming/identity plane before an assessment score means the same thing across
them. The SCuBA/Zero-Trust-Assessment pair is the sharpest available
illustration of that principle inside a *single* vendor's stack: even
Microsoft, which controls both tools, did not converge them into one
assessment, because a compliance-baseline check and a maturity assessment are
structurally different questions. Multiply that by every other CSP an agency
operates — each of which offers its own native posture and compliance
tooling — plus any on-premises virtualization estate, and "run every vendor's
native tool and call it whole-agency Zero Trust" produces exactly as many
disconnected reports as there are vendors, not one agency-level answer.

**The governance principle this reinforces: agency-level Zero Trust ownership
cannot be delegated to any single CSP's assessment tool, no matter how good
that tool is.** A CSP assessing its own platform is necessarily scoped to its
own platform; it has no visibility into, and no structural incentive to
reconcile against, the other CSPs, the network layer, or the virtualization
estate the agency also runs. The agency — not any vendor — is the only party
positioned to hold one Zero Trust posture across all of them, which is
exactly the reconciliation work §2 describes and no per-CSP tool can
substitute for.

Practical guidance for the specific SCuBA / Zero Trust Assessment case:

- **Keep ScubaGear for BOD-25-01** — it is the tool the directive actually
  names, including the M365 workloads the Zero Trust Assessment does not
  touch.
- **Add the Zero Trust Assessment for maturity breadth** across Intune,
  Azure, and Purview — surfaces SCuBA's baseline does not reach.
- **Reconcile both at the control level** (NIST SP 800-53 / FedRAMP
  Moderate) rather than expecting either tool's output to substitute for the
  other's; they use different finding identifiers and severity models.
- **One federal caveat:** in a GCC-class tenant, feature availability
  narrows — the companion paper's Principle Five (§8) covers modeling the
  federal cloud boundary explicitly — so a Zero Trust Assessment run there
  is structurally capped in what it can even measure for Identity, Devices,
  and Networks without agency-built analytics on top, worth knowing before
  treating its score as definitive.
- **None of this — for Microsoft's ecosystem or any other CSP's — substitutes
  for the agency-level reconciliation in §2 above.** Two well-run Microsoft
  tools are still a Microsoft-scoped answer, not an agency-wide one.

### 4. Conclusion

A whole-agency Zero Trust score is only as real as the architecture behind
it. Network, every CSP an agency operates, and any on-premises virtualization
estate have to resolve against one authoritative naming and identity plane
before three separate assessments can be added together and mean anything as
a single number — and once that unification exists, it is itself the
highest-value target in the estate and has to be governed accordingly. The
Microsoft SCuBA / Zero Trust Assessment worked example makes the point
concrete in miniature: even inside one vendor's own ecosystem, two
well-built, complementary, free assessment tools do not converge into a
whole-agency answer, because neither was built to see past its own platform.
No CSP's native tool — however good — is scoped to do that, and none ever
will be, because reconciling across CSPs, the network layer, and a
virtualization estate is definitionally an agency-level responsibility, not
a vendor one. Horse before the cart: unify Network, CSPs, and VMware into one
governed architecture first, and let assessment confirm it — not the other
way around. The governance principles for doing that unification work, and
for hardening what it creates, are the subject of the companion paper, *[Zero
Trust Governance Principles](zero-trust-governance-principles.qmd)*.
